newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE - Time to send in the Internet Mounties?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Time to send in the Internet Mounties?.

text.p: You could call it the World Wild Web because on the Internet just about anything goes.
That is just how many people like it -- an arena mostly, though not completely, beyond the long arm of the government and the regulatory-minded.
Yet some keen minds are working on ways to send in the Cyber Mounties to bring a little law and order to the new digital frontier.

Legal beagles have grown fascinated with the burgeoning personal and commercial life on the Internet and what they see as a need to bring law and order to a place that defies traditional definitions and boundaries.

A number of court actions have been taken against sites and content on the Internet, but legal experts have said the global computer network is likely to prove impervious to the laws of any one country.

For example, if a company claims it was libelled on the Internet from someone posting a message from a computer in Britain, where would the offended party file its case -- in Britain or its home country?
That sort of thing is small potatoes compared to problems that could crop up soon. While child pornography is a growing concern, a number of other issues are waiting to explode.

What happens if local authorities want to ban gambling in a country where citizens have access to gambling houses on the Internet? What if a bank chartered in one country accepts customers from another and breaks local financial regulations?
These questions lack simple answers because old notions of legal systems defined by national borders have gone the way of 2,400-baud modems, the old slow links between telephone lines and computers.

"Global computer-based communications cut across territorial borders, creating a new realm of human activity and undermining the feasibility -- and legitimacy -- of applying laws based on geographic boundaries," wrote David Johnson and David Post in a paper entitled "Law and Borders -- The Rise of Law in Cyberspace."
The paper, which can be found at the Washington-based Cyberspace Law Institute (www.cli.org), basically advocated that Cyberspace be considered a separate entity unrelated to the "real" world.

"Many of the jurisdictional and substantive quandaries raised by border-crossing electronic communications could be resolved by one simple principle: conceiving of Cyberspace as a distinct "place" for purposes of legal analysis by recognising a legally significant border between Cyberspace and the 'real world'," the authors stated.

Some have suggested that a Law of the Sea-type convention could be drafted, requiring international cooperation. It would also be resisted by many dedicated Web heads who resist bureaucracy in an arena blessedly free of all that.

Others have suggested more of a self-regulatory scheme where a Web court could be set up, with the ultimate punishment being banishment. The court could issue Internet certificates with a unique number that could be withdrawn from people who violated Web "netiquette."
But even that would be resisted by many who smelled a Big Brother-type system, complete with an all-controlling personal identification number.
